text:
My opponent is right that a ban needs measurements to be lifted, and that tripwires have fired against earlier dangers. But the case rests on a concession: their own source, an early advocate of the if-then approach, says one should not expect voluntary commitments to stop companies racing. That is the race the statement targets. Tests that arrive alongside a binding line are useful. Tests alone leave the line in the lab's hands.

They call a ban a long shot. Yet their remedy, laws that make the "then" binding, is also a political fight, and a law that binds a halt is a prohibition by another name. The honest choice is which binding line to push for. A line drawn at the destination, with the burden of proof on builders, stays clear even when tests are ambiguous or models notice they are being tested.

sources.title: If-Then Commitments for AI Risk Reduction (Karnofsky, Carnegie Endowment, 2024)
sources.quote: in the long run, one should not expect voluntary commitments to stop companies from racing toward large commercial opportunities

review_note: Corrected in review at the advocate's request: “a co-author of” became “an early advocate of”, which is what the other side's opening and its source support.
